classification.difficultyReason: Identify two side lengths and a rectangular area, explain a supplied four-region area identity, then connect that explicitly scaffolded dissection to the already taught difference-of-squares product. Geometric-to-algebraic coordination is required, while the decomposition and target identity are supplied.

spec.description: Portrait rectangle ACEG with vertical BF and horizontal HD intersecting at J; the whole left rectangle ABFG is shaded. Unequal labelled segments require free-form TikZ rather than a fraction-grid template.
spec.mathematics: AC=a, BC=b, CD=a, DE=b; AB=a-b and AG=a+b. ACDH is a square of area a² and JDEF is a square of area b².
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens and the requested shaded region are visible; no derived lengths or areas are supplied.

children.label: c
children.prompt: What is the area of the shaded region?

answer.short: The first two regions together form the whole rectangle $ACEG$. Removing the two rectangles in its right column leaves $ABFG$.
answer.worked: The horizontal line $HD$ divides $ACEG$ into $ACDH$ and $HDEG$. The right column consists of $BCDJ$ and $JDEF$. Subtracting those two regions from the whole rectangle leaves exactly the shaded rectangle $ABFG$.

children.label: e
children.prompt: What has this got to do with the difference of squares expansions?

answer.short:
$(a-b)(a+b)=a^2-b^2$

The shaded area gives a geometric demonstration of the identity.
answer.worked:
$\begin{align*}(a-b)(a+b)&=a^2+ab-ab-b^2\\(a-b)(a+b)&=a^2-b^2\end{align*}$
The same shaded area is both the product of its side lengths and the difference of the two square areas, demonstrating the difference-of-squares identity.
